parts.problem_md:
Read Text A and Text B in the[ insert](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/english-language/cie/past-papers/paper/ppr_SmtFXRk7CbmXfbRM/?pdf=https%3A%2F%2Fpastpapers.co%2Fcie%2FIGCSE%2FEnglish-First-Language-0500%2F2023-Oct-Nov%2F0500_w23_in_23.pdf&type=resource&resourceIndex=0) and then answer Section A, Question 1(a) and 1(b).

**1(a)** Reread this extract from **Text B:**

"The first major side effect of excessive ambition is the tendency to focus too stubbornly on one particular vision or end goal. For example, if you set out to make your fortune by the time you're 30, everything that doesn't immediately appear to get you closer to that goal may seem useless to you and you miss out on the enjoyment of the 'journey'. Experts suggest that relationships are more important than ambition when determining a person's ability to succeed. Being ambitious often makes you inherently more selfish, driving you to pursue individual goals at the possible expense of your family, friends and community."

**Use your own words** to evaluate the writer's attitude to ambition. Give details from the text to justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

In this extract the writer's attitude to ambition is wary and quietly critical. Ambition is treated almost as a condition with a "side effect", a clinical word that frames it as something potentially harmful rather than admirable. The writer warns that it makes people "focus too stubbornly" on a single goal, so that anything else "may seem useless" and the "enjoyment of the 'journey'" is lost - a narrowing of life rather than an enriching of it. The criticism then turns moral: ambition makes people "inherently more selfish", pursuing personal goals "at the possible expense of your family, friends and community". By citing "experts" who rank "relationships" above ambition, the writer presents this scepticism as reasoned rather than merely personal.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - wary / critical - ambition has a damaging "side effect"
> - sees it as narrowing - people "focus too stubbornly" and lose the "enjoyment of the 'journey'"
> - morally concerned - ambition makes people "inherently more selfish"
> - alert to social cost - goals pursued at the "expense of your family, friends and community"
> - measured / reasoned - draws on "experts" who value "relationships" more highly
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> The response evaluates how the writer's cautionary attitude is constructed within this extract rather than simply labelling it "negative". It notes the clinical framing of "side effect", traces the move from a practical criticism (narrow focus) to a moral one (selfishness), and shows how the appeal to "experts" makes the scepticism feel reasoned. Short phrases are quoted verbatim and tied to specific points about tone, so the judgement stays grounded in the given extract throughout
> 
> **Reading**
> 
> | Level | Marks | Description |
> |---|---|---|
> | 3 | 4-5 | Clear evaluation of the writer's attitude to ambition with relevant support from the extract |
> | 2 | 2-3 | Some understanding of the writer's attitude with some supporting detail |
> | 1 | 1 | Limited understanding of the writer's attitude |
> | 0 | 0 | No creditable content |

**1(a)** Reread this extract from **Text A:**

"Podcasts have been around for years, but I have only recently discovered what a great use of time they are. Most of my work colleagues always seemed to have their earphones in, but what were they listening to? I had heard of podcasts. I knew they were a kind of audio programme you could subscribe to and listen to, for example on your smartphone, whenever you like. I had not realised how much I would enjoy them, especially when faced with administrative tasks in the office. I whizz through those boring tasks now."

**Use your own words** to evaluate the writer's attitude to podcasts. Give details from the text to justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

In this extract the writer's attitude to podcasts is enthusiastic and faintly evangelical. They are presented as a discovery that has changed her routine: she calls them "a great use of time" and admits she "had not realised how much I would enjoy them". Her surprise gives the praise a convincing, first-hand quality, as though she is sharing a secret others have missed. The detail that colleagues "always seemed to have their earphones in" hints at mild self-reproach for being late to something everyone else already valued. The attitude is also practical: podcasts make even dull "administrative tasks" bearable, and the lively claim that "I whizz through those boring tasks now" shows her delight that they turn wasted, tedious moments into something productive and enjoyable.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - enthusiastic / converted - podcasts are "a great use of time"
> - pleasantly surprised - she "had not realised how much I would enjoy them"
> - self-aware / slightly late to them - colleagues "always seemed to have their earphones in"
> - practical - they make "administrative tasks" bearable
> - energised / upbeat - "I whizz through those boring tasks now"
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> The response evaluates how the writer's attitude is built within this extract, not merely that she is "positive". It reads her surprise as adding sincerity, notes the gentle self-criticism in the reference to her colleagues, and shows how the practical examples turn enthusiasm into persuasion. Short phrases are quoted verbatim and each is used to support a specific point about tone, so the analysis stays anchored to the given extract throughout

parts.problem_md:
Read Text A and Text B in the [insert](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/english-language/cie/past-papers/paper/ppr_gTxF58cBSB8Cfty3/?pdf=https%3A%2F%2Fpastpapers.co%2Fcie%2FIGCSE%2FEnglish-First-Language-0500%2F2023-Oct-Nov%2F0500_w23_in_21.pdf&type=resource&resourceIndex=0) and then answer Section A, Question 1(a) and 1(b).

**1(a)** Reread this extract from **Text A:**

"Empty historic buildings that were once local landmarks now get in the way of new projects (such as repurposing of the land for parks, shops and recreational space) that might offer more benefit to the community. If a building looks old and abandoned and you can't find any good reason to keep it, then you should consider demolishing and replacing it. Buildings often outlive their original purposes. Even when still in use, the enormous cost of repairing some very old buildings can be prohibitive, so they become shabby and unsightly. Some older buildings may still look good on the outside, but have underlying problems such as poor ventilation, outdated wiring and problems with the plumbing. Old buildings also tend to develop weaker foundations, thanks to the materials used in their construction degrading to the point that the structure becomes unstable or unsafe."

**Use your own words** to evaluate the writer's attitude to old buildings. Give details from the text to justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

In this extract the writer's attitude to old buildings is dismissive and impatient. They are framed not as treasures but as problems that "get in the way" of better uses for the land, such as "parks, shops and recreational space". The blunt advice that if you "can't find any good reason to keep it" you "should consider demolishing" reveals an unsentimental, almost businesslike stance, with no concession to history or affection. The writer reinforces this by piling up the language of decay - buildings turn "shabby and unsightly", hide "poor ventilation, outdated wiring" and develop "weaker foundations" until they are "unstable or unsafe". By stressing that repair costs can be "prohibitive", the writer treats demolition as the obvious, common-sense conclusion rather than a loss.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - dismissive / unsentimental - old buildings "get in the way" of more useful projects
> - decisive / blunt - advises demolition where there is no "good reason to keep it"
> - critical of their condition - "shabby and unsightly", "weaker foundations", "unstable or unsafe"
> - pragmatic about cost - repair is "prohibitive"
> - progress-focused - the land could "offer more benefit to the community"
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> The response goes beyond simply stating that the writer is "negative" to evaluate how the attitude is built within this extract. It tracks the movement from the buildings being an obstacle, to the blunt recommendation to demolish, to the accumulation of decay and cost. Short quoted phrases are woven in verbatim and are used to support a precise reading of tone (dismissive, impatient, pragmatic), rather than being dropped in without comment. The judgement is rooted only in the given extract
>

>

> |---|---|---|
> | 3 | 4-5 | Clear evaluation of the writer's attitude to old buildings with relevant support from the extract |
> | 2 | 2-3 | Some understanding of the writer's attitude with some supporting detail |

Read Text A and Text B in the [insert](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/english-language/cie/past-papers/paper/ppr_pRZzYFR6WdWkxVQR/?pdf=https%3A%2F%2Fpastpapers.co%2Fcie%2FIGCSE%2FEnglish-First-Language-0500%2F2023-May-June%2F0500_s23_in_23.pdf&type=resource&resourceIndex=0) and then answer Section A, Question 1(a) and 1(b).

**1(a)** Reread this extract from **Text A:**

"Budding footballer 10-year-old Ranit Myska, has already played in several international tournaments in Spain and Singapore, organised by his training academy in India. His father, a doctor, funds his training and his foreign travel, and believes that his son benefits hugely from such opportunities. 'I know some parents think I'm insane,' he says, 'and it costs a lot in my time and money but the relentless emphasis on academics when I was young wasn't healthy either.' Ranit's ambition is to join a major football team's programme when he's 15, so he's dedicated and committed to his rigorous training, but he's also doing well in school. 'The determination he's developing in his football has spilled over into his academic work,' says his father. 'There's no downside for him, despite the arduous training and the sacrifices we make as a family.'"

**Use your own words** to evaluate Ranit's father's attitude to his son's intensive sports training. Give details from the text to justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Ranit's father is confident and wholehearted in his support, convinced that intensive training benefits his son with no real drawbacks. He "believes that his son benefits hugely from such opportunities", a strong claim that frames the training as a clear advantage rather than a gamble. He is aware that others doubt him - "I know some parents think I'm insane" - but is unshaken, defending his choice by arguing that "the relentless emphasis on academics" in his own childhood "wasn't healthy either". This suggests he sees sport as a healthier path than pure study. He also reframes the training as broadly beneficial, claiming the "determination" Ranit develops has "spilled over into his academic work". His insistence that "there's no downside for him" reveals an unreservedly positive attitude, though his admission of the "sacrifices we make as a family" shows he is not entirely blind to its cost.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - Wholehearted belief in the benefits: his son "benefits hugely from such opportunities"
> - Confident and undeterred by criticism: "I know some parents think I'm insane"
> - Justifies his choice against academic pressure: "the relentless emphasis on academics" "wasn't healthy either"
> - Sees wider gains beyond sport: determination has "spilled over into his academic work"
> - Unreservedly positive: "there's no downside for him", while still noting the "sacrifices we make as a family"
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> This response shows clear understanding of Ranit's father's attitude by identifying its central feature - his confident, wholehearted approval - and supporting it with evidence drawn only from the extract. It does more than label the attitude: it explains how he defends his choice against criticism and how he reframes the training as beneficial beyond the pitch. The reading of "benefits hugely", "no downside" and the admission of family "sacrifices" shows engagement with how his conviction, and its one small qualification, are conveyed through his own words, which lifts the answer into the top level.
>

> |---|---|---|
> | 3 | 4-5 | Clear understanding of Ranit's father's attitude with relevant support from the extract |
> | 2 | 2-3 | Some understanding of Ranit's father's attitude with some supporting detail |

Read Text A and Text B in the [insert](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/english-language/cie/past-papers/paper/ppr_5dxt8Qc7Ffdfxsc9/?pdf=https%3A%2F%2Fpastpapers.co%2Fcie%2FIGCSE%2FEnglish-First-Language-0500%2F2023-May-June%2F0500_s23_in_22.pdf&type=resource&resourceIndex=0) and then answer Section A, Question 1(a) and 1(b).

**1(a)** Reread this extract from **Text A:**

"Yesterday, after complaints I'd made to an online retailer for their very poor customer service, I finally received an email in reply. 'At last,' I thought, 'an apology.' And indeed, it was an apology of sorts: a careful set of stock phrases which expressed some limited awareness of their shortcomings with a flourish at the end, hoping that I would 'return very soon to purchase from our unique range of bestselling rugs and soft furnishings.' Now, I know saying sorry is never easy, but I was left with the impression that this writer had been schooled in some business training session that taught employees how to turn an apology into a marketing tool!"

**Use your own words** to evaluate the writer's attitude to the retailer's apology. Give details from the text to justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

The writer's attitude to the retailer's apology is sceptical and unimpressed: she sees it as hollow and self-serving rather than sincere. Her initial hope is clear in "At last,' I thought, 'an apology'", but it is quickly deflated. Calling it "an apology of sorts" signals she does not accept it as the real thing, and "a careful set of stock phrases" implies it is formulaic and impersonal, expressing only "some limited awareness" of fault. Her sharpest criticism is that the message ends by urging her to buy more goods, which exposes its true purpose. The phrase "schooled in some business training session" suggests apologising has been reduced to a learned technique, and her summary that it turns "an apology into a marketing tool" makes her contempt plain. The closing exclamation mark adds a note of exasperated mockery.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - Hopeful at first, then disappointed: "At last,' I thought, 'an apology'"
> - Dismissive that it is genuine: it is only "an apology of sorts"
> - Critical of its formulaic, impersonal nature: "a careful set of stock phrases"
> - Suspicious of its motive: it expresses only "some limited awareness" of fault
> - Scornful that it is really a sales pitch: "schooled in some business training session" turning apology into "a marketing tool"
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> This response shows clear understanding of the writer's attitude by identifying its central feature - her scepticism that the apology is sincere - and supporting it with evidence drawn only from the extract. It tracks the shift from initial hope ("At last") to disappointment, and explains why each phrase generates her distrust rather than simply quoting. The reading of "stock phrases", "an apology of sorts" and "a marketing tool" shows engagement with how the writer's contempt is conveyed through specific word choices and tone, including the mocking exclamation, which lifts the answer into the top level.
> 
> **Reading**
> 
> | Level | Marks | Description |
> |---|---|---|
> | 3 | 4-5 | Clear understanding of the writer's attitude with relevant support from the extract |
> | 2 | 2-3 | Some understanding of the writer's attitude with some supporting detail |

Read Text A and Text B in the [insert](https://www.savemyexams.com/igcse/english-language/cie/past-papers/paper/ppr_5HbnjSpGrwQ9fXsX/?pdf=https%3A%2F%2Fpastpapers.papacambridge.com%2Fdirectories%2FCAIE%2FCAIE-pastpapers%2Fupload%2F0500_s23_in_21.pdf&type=resource&resourceIndex=0) and then answer Section A, Question 1(a) and 1(b).

**1(a)** Reread this extract from **Text B:**

"Paolo says the summers are difficult for locals. The traffic is suffocating, and the pavements are crowded and hot. 'At least the city's facilities are open all year now. Everything used to close in the winter. Most of the cultural events and festivals are still organised around the visitors. We've spent decades "improving the visitor experience", as they say.' Paolo betrays only a hint of irony."

**Use your own words** to evaluate Paolo's attitude to tourism in his city. Give details from the text to justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Paolo's attitude to tourism is ambivalent: appreciative of its benefits but quietly frustrated by its costs. He concedes a genuine gain when he notes "the city's facilities are open all year now", whereas "everything used to close in the winter" - a practical improvement he is willing to acknowledge. Yet his frustration is just as real. Calling the summer traffic "suffocating" suggests the influx feels oppressive, and his remark that events are "still organised around the visitors" implies locals come second. The word "still" hints at long-standing resentment. His ironic reference to "improving the visitor experience" reveals scepticism about the official language of tourism, and the narrator's note that he "betrays only a hint of irony" shows his criticism is measured rather than openly hostile - he is restrained, but unconvinced.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - Appreciative of practical benefits: "the city's facilities are open all year now" where "everything used to close in the winter"
> - Frustrated by overcrowding: the summer traffic is "suffocating"
> - Resentful that locals come second: events are "still organised around the visitors"
> - Sceptical of official rhetoric: ironic reference to "improving the visitor experience"
> - Measured rather than openly hostile: he "betrays only a hint of irony"
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> This response shows clear understanding of Paolo's attitude by capturing its central feature - its ambivalence - and weighing both sides with evidence drawn only from the extract. It does more than label the attitude: it explains what generates the appreciation (year-round facilities) and what generates the frustration (overcrowding, events arranged for visitors). The close reading of "suffocating", "still organised around the visitors" and the "hint of irony" shows engagement with how attitude is conveyed through specific word choices rather than stated outright, which is what lifts the answer into the top level.
>

**1(a)** Reread this extract from **Text B:**

"I’d worked for months to cultivate one prospective client,’ explains Jaz. ‘Everyone knew winning a big order from that client could be a deciding factor in which of us from the international sales team got promoted. Then I discover from a junior colleague that Ravi’s also trying to net this wealthy individual, even though Ravi knew I was already in pursuit! I knew if I ignored the situation, he’d just seal the deal, profiting shamelessly from all my slaving away, and our boss would promote Ravi. But if I’d directly confronted Ravi, it could’ve made me look petty and selfish. At the time, I calculated the best way to fight back was to be just as devious as Ravi."

**Use your own words** to evaluate Jaz’s attitude to work. Give details from the text to justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Jaz demonstrates a hard-working and motivated attitude to work, having “worked for months” to secure a wealthy client which might lead to a promotion, demonstrating that they are ambitious. The use of competitive language such as “winning”, “net” and “pursuit” suggests they feel like work is a contest or battle, but that they also feel threatened and anxious about being treated unfairly, fearing that their colleague might “seal the deal” and take credit for their effort. Ultimately, they reveal a ruthless and calculating attitude, deciding that the only way to succeed is to “fight back” and be “just as devious” themselves.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Responses *might* use the following:
> 
> - competitive: winning a big order, I was already in pursuit, trying to net
> - ruthless/determined: calculated the best way to fight back was to be just as devious
> - ambitious/focussed: could be a deciding factor in which of us got promoted, wealthy individual
> - hard-working/motivated: worked for months to cultivate, all my slaving away
> - feels unfairly treated/anxious: everyone knew, profiting shamelessly, made me look petty and selfish
> 
> **Why this answer would get full marks**
> 
> This answer would get full marks because it demonstrates clear understanding of the focus of the text and uses evaluative vocabulary in the student’s own words to label Jaz’s attitude. Each point is supported with relevant, concise detail from the text and the answer explains what the quote shows about the writer’s attitude. Finally, the answer covers a good range of points.
